The coordinate identities \(\hat s=\hat\theta\), \(\hat n=-\hat r\), and \(\hat\ell=\hat z\) apply everywhere, but \(\hat s\) and \(\hat n\) change spatial direction around the circle. The phrase “the same everywhere” should be understood as these identities, not constant Cartesian vector directions. The pressure plots are qualitative and reproduce the source point order and trends.

Reynolds averaging does not itself introduce a known turbulent viscosity: it introduces the divergence of the Reynolds stress, represented here by \(f_t\). An eddy-viscosity relation is an additional closure model. The original wording is retained.

The final limitation describes a stationary time-average decomposition. Reynolds averaging more generally can use an ensemble mean that varies with time, so the statement that Reynolds averaging is possible only for stationary flow is too restrictive.

The unsteady Bernoulli integral in (5.79) has the wrong sign. With \(s\) increasing from 1 to 2, \(\partial B/\partial s=-\rho\,\partial U/\partial t\), hence \(B_2=B_1-\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\rho(\partial U/\partial t)\,ds\). The steady limit is still \(B_1=B_2\).

Equation (5.80) omits gravity on both sides of the displayed implication. It is a version of Navier–Stokes with gravity neglected (or with its conservative contribution absorbed into a modified pressure), whereas (5.77) writes gravity explicitly.
